title: Tokenization to Transfer: Do Genomic Foundation Models Learn Good Representations?
claim: Initialization quality is governed by tokenizer choice, while gains from pretraining vary widely and depend on the tokenizer type.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, scatter plots with diagonal no-gain line
description: Three side-by-side scatter plots (A: NT Benchmark Histone, B: GUE Benchmark, C: Genomics Benchmark) share a legend on top. Legend colors are Character (red/orange), BPE (green) and K-mer (blue). Each panel plots random-initialization score on the x-axis against pretrained score on the y-axis, with a dashed gray diagonal marking no improvement. Each point is a genomic foundation model, such as Mistral, Caduceus, HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2, GENA-LM or NT-500M, labeled by name and a colored delta value showing the pretraining gain. Marker size reflects parameter count. Blue and green points sit well above the diagonal, while red character models cluster to the right and near or below the diagonal. The eye goes first to the large colored dots and the labeled deltas.
caption: Tokenizer choice determines random baseline quality, while pretraining gains are more complex. A comparison of an averaged performance of identical models with random initialization (x-axis) versus pretrained (y-axis) across (A) NT Benchmark (12 histone and enhancer tasks), (B) GUE (7 task categories), and (C) Genomic Benchmarks (8 tasks). Points above the diagonal indicate a benefit from pretraining. Finding: The random baseline performance is strongly determined by the tokenizer, with character models (Orange) consistently outperforming subword models (Blue, Green). In contrast, the performance gains from pretraining are largest for subword models (NT-500M ∆+ 0.242 MCC on GUE) but are highly variable for character models. Marker size is scaled with the number of model parameters.
abstract: The success of Large Language Models has inspired the development of Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs) through similar pretraining techniques. However, the relationship between pretraining performance and effectiveness in downstream genomic tasks remains unclear. Additionally, the high computational cost of pretraining raises questions about its cost-efficiency. To assess the usefulness of pretraining in genomics, we evaluated seven different GFMs across 52 diverse genomic tasks, comparing them to their counterparts with randomly initialized weights. Across benchmarks, we find that randomly initialized models provide surprisingly strong baselines and tokenizer and architecture choices strongly shape both these baselines and the gains from pretraining. Specifically, character‑token models often match or exceed the performance of larger pretrained k‑mer or BPE models, whereas subword models appear to benefit from pretraining. We also find that the evaluated GFMs fail to capture clinically relevant genetic mutations, with embeddings and log‑likelihood ratios showing limited sensitivity to annotated variants. For the tasks we study, these results suggest that current NLP‑style pretraining strategies provide modest, tokenizer‑gated improvements over strong random baselines and motivate more biologically informed tokenization and variant‑aware objectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/m42-health/gfm-random-eval.
